question: Let U be a unitary on n system qubits and a auxiliary qubits. For a strictly positive real alpha, define B=(<0^a| tensor I)U(|0^a> tensor I). State what it means for U to encode a system operator A exactly or with induced-operator-norm error at most epsilon>=0. Give the matrix dimensions and derive the scalar entry condition equivalent to exact encoding. Explain why division by alpha needs its stated premise.
reference_answer: U has dimension2^(n+a) square. B and A have dimension2^n square. Exact encoding means A=alpha B; approximate encoding means ||A-alpha B||<=epsilon in the induced Euclidean operator norm. Exact equality is equivalent to each clean entry U((0,i),(0,j))=A(i,j)/alpha because alpha>0, hence nonzero. The norm error is zero exactly for equal operators. Positivity is a scale convention, while nonzero is the logical premise needed for division; at alpha=0 the undivided equation reduces to A=0 and does not determine B, so the divided equivalent statement is not defined. The scale is not assumed optimal, and no efficient implementation follows from the existence of U.

question: A circuit acts on a signal register S, a workspace W and a data register D, starting S,W at zero. The signal value0 is called success. Explain the additional mathematical promise needed to call W clean on every successful branch. Does knowing only the smaller submatrix obtained by projecting BOTH S and W to zero imply that promise? Give a two-dimensional workspace counterexample, and explain which auxiliary qubits still occupy physical space.
reference_answer: Workspace cleanliness on signal success means that for every data input v, projecting the final state onto S=0 leaves a vector of the form |0>_S|0>_W tensor T v, with no component at S=0,W nonzero. This is an extra restriction on success-sector amplitudes. The doubly projected submatrix alone fixes only the W=0 component and does not constrain W nonzero. Counterexample: take signal and data one-dimensional and let W be a qubit with unitary R=[[cos t,-sin t],[sin t,cos t]],0<t<pi/2. Its doubly projected block is the scalar cos t, an exact legitimate block for that scalar target. Yet R|0>=cos t|0>+sin t|1>, so workspace is not clean even though signal success is certain. Both signal and workspace qubits enlarge the physical unitary, regardless of whether a resource ledger counts them in different roles. Projection is not itself uncomputation; a separately proved clean-workspace promise cannot be inferred just from the scalar clean submatrix.

question: Suppose unitaries U and V have clean blocks A and B on the same data space. Explain why applying V then U with DISJOINT auxiliary registers initialized at zero yields clean block AB. Show concretely why simply reusing a single auxiliary register can fail. Is resetting that register or applying its inverse automatically a free coherent repair?
reference_answer: With independent auxiliary indices, the final all-zero projection fixes each register only at its own factor; summing over the common data index gives sum_k A(i,k)B(k,j), hence AB. Reusing one register instead introduces paths that leave its zero sector under V and return under U. A minimal example has one-dimensional data and a qubit auxiliary, U=V=X. Each individual clean block is <0|X|0>=0, so AB=0, but <0|X X|0>=1. Resetting an entangled auxiliary is not unitary and may erase coherence; it does not turn the same-register product into the coherent operator AB for free. Applying V inverse cancels V on the entire state and can also erase the desired action, not merely its garbage. A different coherent cleanup construction must be proved under its own promises and charged; disjoint fresh registers give the straightforward product construction. The matrix product of already-extracted blocks alone is not a proof of a particular same-register circuit.

U=V=X zero individual blocks but composite clean block1
Reset nonunitary and inverse can erase desired action; no free cleanup claim

assumptions: U,V unitary with unit normalization for simplicity

conventions: Product applies right factor first (B), then left (A), to the system
Clean branch requires all-zero ancilla before each factor

The X/X same-register witness creates a garbage-return path missed by AB.
